summary: Defines an HTTP authentication scheme for Privacy Pass. Clients can use it to redeem Privacy Pass tokens with an origin server, and origins can use it to challenge clients to present such tokens.

eli5.summary: A website can ask visitors to show a special ticket, and visitors can hand it over, all through normal web messages.

questions: what is the privatetoken http authentication scheme
how does privacy pass token redemption work
what is a privacy pass token challenge
subtitle: How a website challenges a browser for an unlinkable Privacy Pass token, and how the browser hands one back, using ordinary HTTP headers.

tldr.problem: Privacy Pass tokens let a client prove it was able to get a token issued without letting the relying party link that proof to the issuance, but clients and websites need a common way to ask for and present such tokens over HTTP.
tldr.mechanism: An Origin sends a WWW-Authenticate challenge with the PrivateToken scheme carrying a TokenChallenge and a token-key. The Client gets a matching token from an Issuer and redeems it in an Authorization header.
tldr.outcome: A single scheme works across different token issuance protocols, with optional binding to a redemption context and to specific Origins, which supports both interactive and pre-fetched tokens.

today: RFC 9577 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2024 and, per the metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated. It works together with the architecture in RFC 9576 and the issuance protocols in RFC 9578.

sections.title: Privacy Pass Over HTTP
sections.content:
Privacy Pass tokens are unlinkable authenticators. Token Issuers produce them based on authentication, attestation or some earlier action such as solving a CAPTCHA. A Client holding a token can show it was able to get one issued, and the relying party redeeming it (the Origin) cannot link it to the issuance flow.

This document defines a single HTTP authentication scheme named PrivateToken (using the framework in RFC 9110) for redeeming many kinds of Privacy Pass tokens. The Origin challenges with the WWW-Authenticate response header, the Client runs one of the issuance protocols from RFC 9578 to obtain a matching token, and then redeems it by sending an Authorization request header. The architecture itself is in RFC 9576.

The scheme optionally ties tokens to an Origin-chosen context and to specific Origin names. This allows different ways of preventing double-spending, and both interactive (online challenge) and non-interactive (pre-fetched) tokens.
sections.eli5: A club bouncer asks for a stamp. You get the stamp from a different booth that does not tell the bouncer who you are, then you show it at the door.

sections.title: Challenges, Tokens and Headers
sections.content:
A token challenge is carried in WWW-Authenticate: PrivateToken challenge="...", token-key="...". The challenge parameter is a base64url TokenChallenge and is required. The token-key is the base64url public key for the issuance protocol and MAY be omitted if Clients get the Issuer key out of band. An optional max-age gives the seconds the challenge is accepted. Base64url values MUST include padding. A response can hold several challenges, which should be functionally equivalent, and the Origin can list its preferred one first.

The default TokenChallenge begins with a 2-octet token_type that names the issuance protocol; Clients MUST ignore challenges with token types they do not support. It then carries issuer_name, a redemption_context of either 0 or 32 bytes, and origin_info, which is empty or a comma-separated list of Origin names. If origin_info is not empty the Origin MUST list its own name. Server names are a hostname with an optional port (443 if missing) and no userinfo.

The redemption context lets the Origin demand tokens bound to a context, for example a per-request nonce or a value derived from a time window or the Client's ASN.

The default token contains token_type, a 32-octet nonce, a 32-octet challenge_digest (SHA-256 of the TokenChallenge), a token_key_id and an authenticator computed over the preceding fields. It is sent as Authorization: PrivateToken token="...". Unknown parameters MUST be ignored.
sections.eli5: The challenge is a note from the website saying which ticket booth it trusts and what kind of ticket it wants. The ticket carries a random number and a fingerprint of that note, so it only works for that request.

sections.title: Client and Origin Behavior
sections.content:
On receiving a challenge, a Client validates it first: the token type is supported, the structure is well-formed, and if origin_info is non-empty it includes the name of the Origin that sent the challenge (compared case-insensitively). If validation fails the Client MUST NOT fetch or redeem a token.

Clients can cache tokens generated from one challenge. This separates issuance from redemption in time, which improves privacy. A cached token only matches if token_type, issuer_name, redemption_context and origin_info are all the same. Context-bound tokens SHOULD be discarded when state such as cookies is flushed or the network changes.

Clients choose whether to redeem at all. Where tokens only reduce CAPTCHAs, a Client can ignore challenges with some non-trivial probability. Clients SHOULD have a policy limiting how many tokens Origins can cause them to fetch, since a malicious Origin could send many challenges with unique contexts. If several challenges arrive, the Client satisfies exactly one, consistently.

Origins SHOULD minimize the number of challenges sent to a Client context. They SHOULD implement some form of double-spend prevention so the same nonce is not redeemed twice. Origins that share a redemption context, Issuer and origin_info must share their double-spend state.
sections.eli5: The visitor checks the note is really for this website. Tickets are meant to be used once, so the website keeps track of the numbers it has already seen.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
All random values MUST come from a cryptographically secure source. The RFC discusses several attacks:

  • Replay: applications SHOULD constrain tokens to one Origin unless replay is acceptable, and Origins SHOULD use an anti-replay mechanism when redemption has side effects. Replay may be fine for requests that are already linkable, such as 0-RTT data.
  • Reflection: cross-Origin tokens with empty contexts can be reflected by an attacker between an Origin and a Client.
  • Token exhaustion: any Origin in a cross-Origin set can deplete a Client's tokens, so tokens can be scoped to a single Origin or the Client can limit redemptions.
  • Timing correlation: context-bound challenges push issuance and redemption close together, so a colluding Issuer and Origin could link them; Clients MAY add delay.
  • Cross-context linkability: hence the rule to discard context-bound tokens on cookie flush or network change.
sections.eli5: Tickets can be copied, bounced back, or used up by a pushy site, and timing can give you away. The rules say how to use them safely.

sections.title: IANA Registrations and Greasing
sections.content:
IANA registered the PrivateToken authentication scheme and created a Privacy Pass Token Types registry of 2-byte values (maximum 0xFFFF). New entries use the Specification Required policy and list fields such as the token structure, key encoding, whether tokens are publicly verifiable, and the lengths Nk and Nid. RFC 9578 defines entries.

The registry starts with reserved values, including 0x0000, 0x02AA and 0x1132, used for greasing, inspired by RFC 8701. Origins SHOULD include random reserved token types in challenges with some non-trivial probability, and SHOULD sometimes skip challenging when tokens are optional, so that Clients stay able to handle unknown types and Clients that cannot redeem. Appendix A provides test vectors for challenges, tokens and headers.
sections.eli5: Now and then a website sends a fake, made-up kind of ticket request so browsers practice ignoring things they do not understand.
